title: Aurora Shelter ‘Home’
deck: A residential shelter environment shaped around safety, dignity, and a renewed sense of belonging.
story: Experiences in Toledo’s streets and shelters changed my understanding of architecture. In winter, I often saw unhoused residents holding signs asking for a home, and I began to question what happened after they disappeared from those corners.

The 2025 AIA Toledo design competition created an opportunity to confront that question directly through a shelter for unhoused women and children. Conversations with Aurora Project residents made the priorities clear: safety, dignity, privacy, and the ordinary comfort of a place that feels like home.

Rather than reproduce an institutional shelter model, the proposal draws from familiar residential patterns in Toledo. Gardens, protected paths, domestic-scale volumes, and clear thresholds work together to support belonging without reinforcing marginalization. The project’s recognition by Toledo City Council confirmed that architecture can participate in public dialogue and contribute to social healing.

title: Mobile Bridge
deck: A tiny library that connects river, park, and forest through a productive civic bridge.
story_title: A cultural flow belt for a small town.
story: Hyden, Kentucky faces limited employment, population loss, an aging demographic, and the effects of substance abuse. The proposal responds with a vertically stacked productive space where reading, craft, gardening, health support, and collective activity can coexist.

The concept of a mobile bridge links three natural conditions—the river, park, and forest—into a cultural flow belt. Each end becomes a distinct spatial hub while the center acts as a shared threshold between landscape and town.

Over the river, stepped bookshelves rise toward a viewing level above a glass floor. Toward the forest, reading terraces and a meditation area create quiet visual continuity with the trees. The park-facing zone supports workshops, medical and psychological services, and sustainable agriculture, turning a small library into civic infrastructure.

title: Green Shell
deck: A porous urban pavilion that turns a generative shell into shade, habitat, and public room.
story_title: A responsive canopy between city and ecology.
story: Green Shell brings together organic morphology, digital fabrication logic, and public space. Conceived for Toledo, the pavilion creates an urban oasis where filtered light, shadow, planting, and movement define the experience.

The pavilion is treated as a responsive organism rather than a freestanding object. Its placement and openings establish a localized microclimate while maintaining visual continuity with the surrounding landscape.

A Rhino and Grasshopper workflow transforms a continuous surface into a network of nodes and hollow triangular panels. The porous canopy filters sunlight, frames views, and supports native planting below, making environmental performance legible through form.

title: Germination
deck: A formal system translating the growth logic of white dulcamara into architectural structure.
story: Germination begins with the biological morphology of white dulcamara: an upward trajectory defined by stability, rapid expansion, and unpredictable directional shifts.

Botanical anatomy is mapped to architectural elements. Root becomes pedestal, stem becomes vertical support, branches become cantilevered extensions, and the flower bloom culminates as a spatial volume.
The study does not imitate the plant’s appearance. Instead, it extracts a rule set from growth and tests how organic vitality can meet the discipline of structural geometry.

title: Flower in the Rock
deck: A study of fragile inhabitation emerging from heavy, eroded terrain.
story: Flower in the Rock explores the interface between architecture and raw natural forces, taking inspiration from plants that emerge from seemingly barren stone.

Layered corrugated cardboard forms a concave cliff with dramatic protrusions and crevices. Light timber interventions act as the flower: viewing platforms cantilever outward, dwellings nest into recesses, and a skeletal frame reaches above the peak.
The material contrast produces the central tension of the model—heavy earth against fragile architecture, permanence against growth, and shelter against exposure.

title: Helix Tower
deck: Equal-length elements rotate around a circle to test balance, repetition, and vertical force.
story: Helix Tower explores a simple geometric operation: equal-length wooden elements are positioned tangentially to a circle and rotated upward at a constant angle.
The repeated rule creates spatial stacking without abandoning legibility. Each element depends on the next, turning serial rotation into both structural logic and visual rhythm.
The final model stands vertically on a single plane, testing how minimal contact and carefully distributed forces can produce architectural equilibrium.

title: Architecture Magazine
deck: An editorial system connecting architectural typologies, image hierarchy, and expressive typography.
story_title: Architecture translated into an editorial voice.
story: This cover series treats editorial design as a form of architectural representation. Each composition combines typographic hierarchy, image cropping, rhythm, and negative space to express a distinct architectural typology.

Urban, residential, interior, and Chinese architecture share a consistent visual system while retaining their own atmosphere. The result is a multidisciplinary exercise in how architecture is framed, sequenced, and communicated to a wider audience.

title: Z-Day: Rise of the Horde
deck: A research facility, viral breach, and reactor failure become the spatial climax of a speculative game world.
story: Set in 2047 during a high-technology nuclear conflict, Z-Day centers on HelixCore, a research facility developing an anti-radiation vaccine. An explosion breaches containment and releases the volatile Nexis-9 virus.

Lead researcher Barr mutates, damages the reactor, and triggers an escalating fusion failure. Agent 1012 enters the facility in response to a distress signal with two spatial objectives: shut down the reactor and seal the site.

The environment is designed as a sequence of pressure, evidence, and revelation. Lighting, circulation, containment chambers, and industrial scale guide the player toward the Part I climax while establishing the world’s larger themes of nuclear fallout, mutation, and technological arms races.
